comments.body:
The fix was submitted to JAX: https://github.com/google/jax/commit/9a098e922aff62a3b49bd673b9518d97ee599248
It adds 2 new optional flags (turned-off by default):

1. jax_share_binary_between_hosts: if flag is enabled the coordinator process (the process with id 0) will share the optimized module with other processes. This will not work if the module contains host callbacks and it might overuse networking since one process will send modules one-by-one to all participants.
2. jax_share_autotune_config_between_hosts: if flag is enabled the coordinator process will share only autotune config with other participants. This flag will increase compilation time by ~1.5x since each participant would need to wait for the coordinator process to compile the module and then compile it again. 

These flags can be combined and then  jax_share_binary_between_hosts will be used for modules without host callbacks, otherwise jax_share_autotune_config_between_hosts will be used.
Great ! Would be amazing if we could get to the on-by-default solution.

After https://github.com/openxla/xla/commit/2500111022fc9791bd9134134258c2606be50c4d autotune shard should be enabled by default.
This flag should fix an original issue.

Thanks @sergachev for implementing autotune sharding!

issue.body:
Opening an issue to help us keep track of this even though the discussion has already been ongoing elsewhere.

When using multi-process execution, XLA compiles each module indepedently for each process. Nondeterministic passes like `triton-autotuner` can produce different results per process, which can lead to different optimizations happening later down the pipeline. If any of those optimizations leads to a different ordering of collectives in the schedule, or a different `is_async` designation for collectives, then there will be deadlocks on the first execution.

The ideal solution would be to compile the module once and broadcast the result to all other processes. I believe @hawkinsp is currently planning to work on this.
issue.title: Nondeterminism in triton-autotuner and others leads to hangs in multi-process gpu execution

issue.body:
🤖 *This description is the authoritative summary and is kept current. The comment thread below is the chronological investigation log, including hypotheses that were later refuted. The original 2026-07-17 report by @ClassicLarry is preserved at the bottom.*

## Root cause (found 2026-08-07)

**NCCL 2.28.9 leaks proxy-op slots on aarch64 and a rank whose pool runs dry deadlocks
silently.** The slot-return path in `ncclProxyGetPostedOps` (proxy.cc:845-852) retries a weak
`__atomic_compare_exchange_n` on the observed value (`while (swap != oldFree)`) instead of the
CAS result; a spurious failure — possible on aarch64 LL/SC, impossible on x86 `lock cmpxchg` —
exits the loop without storing and orphans the entire batch of freed slots. The compiled code is
ldaxr/stlxr with the stlxr success flag never tested, and the starved producer's
`__atomic_exchange_n(&freeOps[i], -1)` spin breaks the reservation while leaving the value
unchanged, so leaks concentrate at exactly the backpressure moments. Measured on a live wedge:
the lagging rank's 2048-slot partition fully leaked, healthy sibling ranks at deficits of
830/446/702 and climbing. When a partition hits zero the rank spins forever in
`ncclLocalOpAppend`, its own progress thread sleeps in `ncclProxyGetPostedOps`, every peer
blocks in the collective, and nothing errors or times out. Fixed upstream in
[NCCL v2.29.3-1](https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl/commit/25368a7f78bae866f29e46938af94fa586c84484);
our stack pins `nvidia-nccl-cu13==2.28.9`. Full evidence chain and the causal A/B:
https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5211016784. Forensic method: `experiments/grug/wedge_forensics/` on the
`mcwitt/7344-minimal-repro` branch.

Still open: `t1nccl` and `ngc-8rack` wedged on stacks with NCCL 2.30.7 (which has the fix), so a
second mechanism may exist at hero scale — unresolved; run the pool forensics on the next live
wedge before theorizing.

## Summary

A 512-GPU JAX/XLA training job (`experiments/grug/moe_hero_fsdp`, 128 nodes × 4 GB200, 8 NVL72
racks, cluster `cw-us-east-08a`, NCCL over MNNVL + IB) **stops making forward progress with no
error on any rank.** All 512 processes stay alive, Iris reports `failures=0`, and nothing ever
times out — measured sit-times of 2296 s, 5590 s, 7203 s and 15710 s with no XLA or NCCL timeout
firing. It does not self-terminate, so anything relying on a crash to trigger recovery waits
forever.

Reproduces on stock `main`, on the upstream NVIDIA JAX container, on FSDP and on expert-parallel
programs, at 48 layers and at 1 layer, on real and synthetic data. Time-to-wedge spans **step 17 to
step ~1290** and tracks **wall-clock**, not step or collective count.

## Reproduction

Verified at
[`121b71af6`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/121b71af645d9078f11b90f181568cdcf0551eaa)
(2026-08-06) with **no modifications** — control run `ctrl48b` was byte-identical to stock `main`
(`git status --porcelain` empty) and wedged twice, at step 33 and step 17.

**Prerequisites:** access to the `marin` Iris cluster, 8 free GB200 racks on `cw-us-east-08a`, and
`WANDB_API_KEY` in the environment.

```bash
git checkout 121b71af6
RID=wedge-repro-$(date -u +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)

uv run --frozen iris --cluster=marin job run --no-wait --enable-extra-resources \
  --target-cluster cw-us-east-08a --priority production \
  --cpu 2 --memory 8GB --disk 32GB --timeout 21600 \
  --job-name "${RID}-coord" -e WANDB_API_KEY "$WANDB_API_KEY" \
  -- python -m experiments.grug.moe_hero_fsdp.launch \
     --run-id "$RID" --dp-racks 8 --num-steps 2000 --version dev --run
```

**What that runs.** 128 nodes × 4 GB200 = 512 GPUs over 8 racks, one process per node driving 4
GPUs. 48 layers, hidden 6144, 128 experts top-4 plus 2 shared, 48 heads / 12 KV, head_dim 128,
seq 4096 with 512 sliding window and global attention every 6 layers,
`attention_implementation="gpu_fa4_cute"`, `moe_implementation="sonic_cute"`, `expert_chunks=4`,
MuonH optimizer, `offload_opt_state=True`, bf16 compute / fp32 params, mesh `replica_axis_size=8` /
`expert_axis_size=1`, batch 1024 seq/rack × 8 = 8192 × 4096 = 33.5M tokens/step, real
(SlimPajama-6B) data. Config: `experiments/grug/moe_hero_fsdp/heuristic.py` (`build_hero_configs`)
and `launch.py`.

**Recommended one-line change.** Stock `main` dispatches with `max_retries_failure=3,
max_task_failures=10`. An automatic retry restarts from step 1 **under the same job ID and run
name**, which makes a wedge look like a slow run and overwrites the state you came to measure. At
the `resources=config.resources` call site in `experiments/grug/moe_hero_fsdp/train.py`, set
`max_retries_failure=0` and `max_task_failures=0` (the latter needs plumbing through
`dispatch_grug_training_run` in `experiments/grug/dispatch.py`, which hardcodes 10) so that one
submission equals one trial.

**Expected outcome.** Wedges in roughly **20–40 minutes**, usually between step 17 and step 200.
Set `--num-steps` well above what you expect to reach — the hazard is on wall-clock, so a low step
budget just ends the run before it can fail. A run reaching ~1000 steps clean is >3× the longest
observed and can be treated as a null.

Note you do not get to choose the failure: the same job produces either this wedge or the
single-rank `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION` of #7956, historically about half and half.

**Two practical notes**, both of which have cost hours here:

- `--target-cluster cw-us-east-08a` is **required**. Iris child jobs inherit the parent's region, so
  without it the GB200 request pins to wherever the coordinator landed and returns
  `unschedulable: no scaling group provides device gpu:gb200`.
- Retrieve logs with `--since-ms` timestamp windows, **not** `--tail`. During a failure the 128
  tasks emit ~15,000 lines/second and the interesting lines leave even a 40,000-line tail in
  seconds.

### Reproducing on the expert-parallel program

The wedge also reproduces on `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep` at 8 racks
(`moe-hero-ep-8rack-20260806`, commit `f8a0c7cba`: 128 nodes / 512 GPUs, `expert_axis_size=64`
intra-rack × `replica_axis_size=8` cross-rack, batch 8192, 48 layers / 128 experts top-4,
`moe_implementation="fixed_all_to_all"`). It ran clean for **5.3 hours / ~1290 steps**, then wedged
with the standard signature — frozen power, all ranks alive, RAS desync
([detail](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5205262921)).

⚠️ **This is not reproducible from stock `main`, and the failure mode is silent.** The shipped EP
launcher hardcodes `HERO_EP_NODES = 16` and `replica_axis_size=1` — **one rack**. A one-rack EP job
has no cross-rack collective at all, so it *cannot* exhibit this failure, and a clean run would be
a null by construction rather than evidence that EP is healthy. Scaling the replica axis across
racks (expert parallelism stays intra-rack) is what makes EP comparable to the FSDP hero at the
same infrastructure scale.

The change is mechanical — thread a `dp_racks` parameter through
`experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/launch.py`, mirroring the FSDP launcher:

```python
    batch_size = dp_racks * HERO_EP_BATCH_SIZE          # was: HERO_EP_BATCH_SIZE
    ...
        replica_axis_size=dp_racks,                     # was: 1
    ...
        replicas=HERO_EP_NODES * dp_racks,              # was: HERO_EP_NODES
    ...
            train_batch_size=batch_size,                # was: HERO_EP_BATCH_SIZE
```

plus a `--dp-racks` click option. **This is not upstream** — it lived in a local worktree for the
run above and would need a PR before anyone else can reproduce it.

## Confirming it is actually the wedge

**Log silence is not evidence.** `iris job logs` on a 128-task gang lags by minutes and
`tqdm_loggable` emits only every ~75–80 s, so a healthy run can look silent for 5+ minutes. Three
false alarms were called this way before the power check was adopted.

| state | util | power | SM clocks |
|---|---|---|---|
| healthy compute | 100 % | 700–1150 W | **varying** 1282–1950 sample to sample |
| recompile / idle | 0 % | 200–230 W | low |
| **wedged** | 100 % | **200–280 W** | **pinned 1950, power frozen to two decimals** |

**Frozen power alone is not sufficient either** — a rank legitimately waiting in a collective, or
waiting on an already-dead peer, produces an identical reading. The criterion is the
**conjunction**: frozen power *and* sustained no-progress *and* a persistent NCCL RAS
operation-count gap *and* `failures=0` with every task alive.

Task paths follow `/marin/${RID}-coord/grug-train-${RID}/<task-index>`, tasks 0–127.

```bash
TRAIN="/marin/${RID}-coord/grug-train-${RID}"

# 1. POWER -- the discriminator. Run TWICE, ~30 s apart, and compare.
for t in 0 16 64 112; do
  uv run --frozen iris --cluster=marin task exec "$TRAIN/$t" --timeout 75 -- \
    nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,utilization.gpu,power.draw,clocks.sm,temperature.gpu \
               --format=csv,noheader
done

# 2. NCCL RAS -- which ranks are lagging
uv run --frozen iris --cluster=marin task exec "$TRAIN/0" --timeout 150 -- python3 -c "
import socket
s = socket.create_connection(('localhost', 28028), timeout=40); s.settimeout(40)
s.sendall(b'verbose status\n')
buf = b''
try:
    while True:
        d = s.recv(65536)
        if not d: break
        buf += d
except Exception: pass
print(buf.decode('utf-8', 'replace'))"
# look for 'MISMATCH  Communicator ranks have different AllReduce operation counts';
# it prints the lagging ranks and their node IPs

# 3. STACKS -- py-spy is preinstalled in every task. rank -> task is rank // 4.
uv run --frozen iris --cluster=marin task exec "$TRAIN/<lagging-task>" --timeout 120 -- \
  bash -c 'PID=$(pgrep -f _callable_runner.py | head -1); $IRIS_VENV/bin/py-spy dump --pid $PID --native'

# 4. NVML health -- expect all clean, which is itself the point
uv run --frozen iris --cluster=marin task exec "$TRAIN/0" --timeout 75 -- \
  nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,ecc.errors.uncorrected.volatile.total,remapped_rows.pending,remapped_rows.failure,clocks_event_reasons.hw_slowdown \
             --format=csv,noheader
```

Two known gaps in this method: wedged GPUs read **34–36 °C** at "100 % util", probably a better
signal, but no healthy-compute temperature baseline was ever collected; and stale telemetry after
an Xid 43 channel reset would look identical, with no monotonic counter available to prove liveness
(`total_energy_consumption` is not a valid query field on this driver).

## Where the divergence is

NCCL RAS shows an **operation-count desync** — some subset of ranks has launched fewer AllReduce
operations than the rest and never catches up. **The lagging unit varies**: a full rack (64 ranks),
two nodes in two different racks (8 ranks), and in two captures a **single GPU**. An earlier claim
in this thread that it is always exactly one rack was an artifact of the first three captures and
is retracted.

py-spy shows **identical stacks on lagging and non-lagging ranks** — every one parked in
`absl::...FutexWaiter::WaitUntil` inside `xla_cuda_plugin.so`, waiting on the PJRT async-execution
queue. So the divergence is **below Python**, in XLA/PJRT/NCCL or on the device, not host
scheduling. RAS's "launched up to operation N" counts NCCL operations enqueued *on the device*, not
Python-level progress. py-spy cannot see NCCL's proxy threads: the process has 1222 OS threads and
py-spy reports only the 8 registered with the interpreter.

## Established

| Finding | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Hazard runs on **wall-clock**, not steps or collectives | An 8× smaller batch ran 3.2× more collectives and ~2.8× more fabric traffic per second, yet took *longer* to wedge (86.8 min). Likelihood ratio ~7:1 vs a per-step model ([detail](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5184323726)) |
| **Not our build of the toolchain** | Reproduces on `nvcr.io/nvidia/jax:26.07-py3` — upstream jax, jaxlib, XLA, CUDA 13.3, NCCL 2.30.7 — with a hard provenance gate confirming `libnccl.so.2` / `libcudart.so.13` / `libcuda.so.1` resolve to image paths, not our venv or any `nvidia-*` wheel. Wedged in ~10 min ([detail](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5201483589)) |
| **Large messages are not required** | At 1 layer the model is ~9B params vs ~360B, so every collective is ~40× smaller — and it still wedges |
| **Vendored CuTe/QuACK kernels are not required** | `ngc-8rack` wedged on `reference` attention + `scatter` MoE with the full conjunction verified (frozen power to two decimals, RAS 504-vs-8 operation-count gap, all ranks alive, ECC clean). Caveat: **1 layer only** — `reference` cannot run at 48. See the attention-axis section |
| **Real data is not required** | Wedges on deterministic synthetic tokens — no GCS, no tokenized cache, no shuffle, no mixture |
| **Not FSDP-specific — collective structure is not the discriminator** | `moe_hero_ep` at 8 racks (`expert_axis_size=64` intra-rack × `replica_axis_size=8`, `fixed_all_to_all` MoE) wedged at ~step 1290 with the identical signature. Same infrastructure scale as the FSDP hero, completely different dominant collective ([detail](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5205262921)) |
| **Two racks are enough** | An earlier EP64 program (launched via `experiments.grug.moe.launch_cw_scale`): 32 tasks × 4 GB200 = 128 GPUs, wedged after step 90, ~20 min per attempt ([detail](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5125585656)) |
| EP is **more robust, not immune** | ~1290 steps to wedge against FSDP's 17–160 at the same scale — a large difference in hazard rate with no difference in outcome |
| The hang **does not self-terminate** | Sat 4.4 h with no XLA collective timeout firing; all tasks still `running` |
| The full 48-layer hero is a **cheap** repro vehicle | Wedges at steps 17–200, ~20–40 min — not the multi-hour vehicle the ladder was built to avoid |

## Ablations that do NOT prevent it

| ablation | result |
|---|---|
| NCCL 2.28.9 → 2.30.7 | wedges |
| `NCCL_LAUNCH_ORDER_IMPLICIT=1` | wedges |
| one process per GPU (vs one process driving four) | wedges (`procgpu2`, step ~152) |
| `NCCL_MNNVL_ENABLE=0` | wedges (probable — caveat in [5205262921](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5205262921)) |
| NVLS on vs off | wedges both ways |
| upstream NVIDIA JAX container | wedges |
| `gpu_fa4_cute` vs plain-XLA `reference` attention | wedges under both — the `reference` side is **1 layer only** (it cannot run at 48). Upstream FA4 itself is untested; see the attention-axis section |
| `sonic_cute` vs `scatter` vs `fixed_all_to_all` MoE | wedges under all three |
| FSDP all-gather vs EP64 all-to-all | wedges under both |
| real vs synthetic data | wedges under both |
| 48 layers vs 1 layer | wedges under both |
| `JAX_ENABLE_PGLE` on vs off, collective-overlap limit 1 vs 4 | wedges across both settings of each |

### The attention axis: what is and is not established

An earlier version of this section claimed "attention implementation is not a factor in either
direction." That was **overstated** — not because the evidence is bad, but because it papered over
which runs actually carry it. Setting it out per-run:

| wedge | attention | layers | allocator noise in the same run? |
|---|---|---|---|
| original report (2026-07-17), `repro-v3`, `oldpureD`, `oldbaseB` | `gpu_fa4_cute` | 48 | no |
| `ctrl48b` ×2, `procgpu2`, `mnnvl0` | `gpu_fa4_cute` | 48 | no |
| `ep-8rack`, and the 2-rack EP64 run (`SCALE_ATTN_IMPL gpu_fa4_cute`) | `gpu_fa4_cute` | 48 | no |
| ladder rung 0 | `gpu_fa4_cute` | **1** | no — this is the "no allocation failure" datapoint |
| ladder rung 1 (`r1recap`) | `reference` | **1** | **yes — 19 events, 145.05 GiB**; stall inferred from progress only |
| ladder rung 2 (`r2synthg`) | `reference` | **1** | **yes — 2 events**, and the allocation was logged *at the exact moment* progress stopped |
| **`ngc-8rack`** (rung 1, NVIDIA container) | `reference` | **1** | **wedge verified directly by the full conjunction** — see below |

The `ngc-8rack` row is the one that carries the weight, so here is its evidence rather than a label.
Frozen power: `task112` GPU0 read **223.00 W in both passes** and GPU2 **207.03 W in both**, still
identical when re-sampled four minutes later, at 100 % util with every clock pinned at 1950 MHz.
RAS: **504 ranks at operation 1208 against 8 ranks at 1206**, plus an intra-rack group at 9464 vs
9447, with the lagging ranks and node IPs named. All ranks alive, `failures=0`, ECC/row-remap/
throttle clean. That is the wedge measured directly, on `reference` attention, on the upstream
NVIDIA container.

So the attention kernel is **not** exonerated only by weak evidence — there is one properly
verified `reference` wedge. But two real gaps remain, and they should not be papered over:

1. **Every wedge at 48 layers has used `gpu_fa4_cute`.** `reference` has only ever run at 1 layer,
   because at 48 layers it materialises a 48 GiB `[B,H,S,S]` score matrix per device and the run
   does not survive (`r25nooffload` was fatal at step 1). Rung-0/1 results have twice failed to
   predict 48-layer behaviour, so this gap is not cosmetic.
2. **Upstream FlashAttention-4 has never been run at all.** `gpu_fa4_cute` is our port (see the
   note above); `gpu_fa4_thd` wraps the genuine `flash_attn.cute.flash_fwd_sm100` /
   `flash_bwd_sm100` kernels and is untested.

Next on this axis: **`gpu_fa4_thd` at 48 layers, 8 racks**, holding everything else at the
`ctrl48b` control. Wedging there would close the question for good; not wedging would implicate our
port specifically and would be the most actionable result the campaign has produced.

Separately: anything in this thread reading as "only happens with `reference`" refers to the
retired 145 GiB allocation red herring below, which is a different claim about a different
observable.

> **What `gpu_fa4_cute` is — read this before concluding anything about FlashAttention.** It is
> **upstream flash-attn-4 with a custom forward kernel on Blackwell**, not a wholesale
> reimplementation and not stock FA4 either.
>
> *Upstream*: `flash-attn-4` is a hard dependency. The backward path is "intentionally close to
> upstream `flash_attn.cute.flash_bwd`" (`_fa4_cute_segmented_bwd.py:37`), reuses upstream's
> `flash_bwd_preprocess` / `flash_bwd_postprocess`, and on SM90 calls upstream `flash_bwd_sm90`
> directly. Masking, `SeqlenInfoQK`, the tile scheduler and block sparsity are all upstream's.
>
> *Ours*: the **forward kernel on SM100**. Upstream's native SM100 forward
> (`flash_attn/cute/interface.py`, 128×128 tiles) is **not** used. Instead the forward is a
> segmented kernel adapted from the CUTLASS CuTe DSL FlashAttention-**v2** Ampere example, carrying
> dynamic lower-bound metadata through the SM80/SM120 segmented fork, at 64×64 tiles with a dense
> BSHD layout rather than upstream's THD interface. `_fa4_cute.py:302` states it plainly: *"This
> Grug port is not that native SM100 kernel."* The fork exists because the hero needs per-token
> segment lower bounds that upstream's `cu_seqlens` interface cannot express.
>
> So the two configurations tested so far are *this hybrid* and *no custom kernel at all*
> (`reference` is pure JAX — two einsums and a softmax). **Upstream's own SM100 forward is
> untested**: `gpu_fa4_thd` wraps the genuine `flash_attn.cute.flash_fwd_sm100` /
> `flash_bwd_sm100`, but it requires fixed-shape THD segment metadata the hero config does not
> currently produce (`NotImplementedError` at `_fa4_thd.py:822`), so running it needs a change to
> how the hero builds its `AttentionMask`, not a config flag.

**Campaign tally (2026-08-05/06):** twelve 8-rack trials — 6 wedge verdicts (`ctrl48b` ×2 at steps
33/17, `procgpu2` ~152, `ngc-8rack` ~115, `ep-8rack` ~1290, `mnnvl0` ~24), 5 censored by #7956
(`affin1` 5, `affin2` 17, `n3full` 76, `nowatch` 2, `nowatch2` 161), 1 config-blocked (`pgle0`).

## Directions that are CLOSED — do not re-open without new evidence

**1. The allocator line of inquiry, and everything downstream of it.**

The parent claim was that the wedge is an allocator failure, prompted by a 145 GiB
`cuMemAllocAsync` OOM logged at the moment a run stopped progressing. That is **an artifact of the
rung-1 `reference`-attention ablation**, which materialises a 48 GiB `[B,H,S,S]` score matrix per
device that FA4 never builds; both observed requests were ~3× that. Rung 0 under FA4 wedges with
**no allocation failure at all**. Two sub-hypotheses were generated to explain the 145 GiB figure,
and both died with it:

- *"Something is materialising full-size state on a single device."* Refuted directly — an
  instrumented dump of the initialised train state gives `per_device_total = 9.87 GiB` logical, so
  the 145 GiB was a compiled temp arena, not persistent state.
- *"`offload_opt_state=True` and `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_ALLOCATOR=cuda_async` are the prime suspects."*
  Neither explains the allocation: it appears under **both** `offload_opt_state` settings (shifting
  the request by ~0.75 GiB and changing only whether the failure is fatal), and the old "cannot run
  with `offload_opt_state=False`" verdict is retracted — it compiles and trains normally under FA4.

> ⚠️ **Cleared of *causing the 145 GiB allocation* is not cleared of *causing the wedge*.** Both
> knobs remain live as wedge factors and are listed under Open below. Do not read this item as
> closing them.

**2. A rank-0 role artifact.** The lagging unit varies across racks and down to single GPUs.

**3. NVIDIA's documented multi-device-single-process `cudaFree` hang.** Its prescribed remedy — one
process per device — does not fix ours (`procgpu2` wedged at step ~152).

**4. The "host-side stall" framing.** Refuted by the identical py-spy stacks above.

**5. "Wedges cluster at `compute_watch` steps (multiples of 20)."** Falsified by the rate series:
the +90 s cost appears once at step 20 and never at 40 or 60, so it is a one-time compile of the
`compute_watch=True` executable, not a recurring event.

**6. `JAX_ENABLE_PGLE=0` at 48 layers.** Config-blocked, not a verdict: the flag verifiably took
effect (the PGLE warm-up curve vanished) but the run OOMed at step 37 requesting ~115 GiB against a
138 GiB limit. Disabling PGLE changes the compiled executable enough to blow up the temp arena, and
any mitigation moves the config away from the control. (PGLE is separately ruled out as *necessary*
— the EP64 program wedges with it off.)

**Rung-0 (1-layer) results have twice failed to predict 48-layer behaviour** — most notably "one
process per GPU ran 1710 steps clean" at rung 0, where the same config wedges at 48 layers. Treat
rung-0 verdicts as hypotheses about the hero, not conclusions about it.

## Open — the surviving hypothesis space

What the ablations above have *not* eliminated is narrow, and three of the four items are shared by
every wedging configuration we have.

**1. The allocator — `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_ALLOCATOR=cuda_async`, never ablated in either wedging
program.** It is set explicitly in the EP64 repro command and forced in the FSDP trainer, so it is
one of the few things common to *all* of them. It is there deliberately: #7012 found it fixed a
real deterministic BFC fragmentation OOM, so it cannot simply be dropped without reintroducing that.
Two caveats for whoever runs this:

- Swapping `cuda_async` → BFC is **not** on-mechanism for NVIDIA's documented stream-ordered
  allocator hazard — neither allocator calls `cudaFree` on the hot path, so the swap does not
  exercise that hazard. It is a legitimate toolchain variation, not a mechanism-directed test, and
  should not be ranked as one.
- **Allocator diagnostics lie under `cuda_async`.** `largest_free_block_bytes` and `bytes_reserved`
  both report `0.00` because they are BFC-allocator fields this allocator does not populate — the
  zeros mean "unimplemented", not "no free block". And `Stats: Limit:` is an accounting value, not
  an enforced ceiling: two independent 200-step runs finished with `peak_in_use` exceeding
  `alloc_cap`.

**2. The driver / GPU firmware.** Driver `595.71.05` is uniform across all 205 GB200 nodes, but
uniformity does not exclude an intermittent defect. This is what the Xid correlation below would
address, and it is the highest-value outstanding check.

**3. The fabric** (MNNVL / IB). `NCCL_MNNVL_ENABLE=0` still wedged, but that is a probable negative
rather than a proven one — `NCCL_DEBUG=WARN` in those runs meant the transport change could not be
confirmed directly, only inferred from a ~35% throughput drop.

**4. `offload_opt_state=False` as a wedge factor** — ladder rung 2.5, genuinely unresolved. It runs
fine, but the attempt was pre-empted by a #7956 fault at step 300 before it could either wedge or
clear the exposure bar.

## Relationship to #7956

#7956 is a **single-rank** `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION`: the rank dies, trips JAX's 300 s
shutdown barrier, and aborts the gang in ~5 minutes. The stated discriminator has been "does a rank
die?" — a wedge sits with `failures=0` and every task alive for hours.

**That distinction may track the reporting path rather than the fault.** #7956 is also the binding
operational constraint here: it censored 5 of the last 11 ablation runs, each before a verdict was
reachable. A run killed by #7956 says nothing about whether that configuration wedges.

## Retired lead — Xid 13 / 43 (superseded by the root cause above; this deadlock produces no Xid)

CoreWeave Grafana carries Xid alerts (@ravwojdyla,
[comment 5201166967](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5201166967)).
**Xid 13** is a user application fault — illegal memory access or **instruction errors**; **Xid 43**
is "GPU stopped processing after a software-induced fault; channel reset". Both were seen on
`s7vpxs64` during 02:03–02:13 UTC, overlapping the `ctrl48b` wedge whose last progress line was
02:11:43.

This would unify both issues: one fault, two presentations depending on whether the runtime
surfaces it — the rank dies (**#7956**), or the channel resets while the process stays alive and
that GPU silently stops advancing its NCCL work (**#7344**). An Xid 43 also fits the py-spy finding
exactly: every host thread looks identical because every rank is waiting on a device that will
never finish.

This is a hypothesis on one correlated timestamp. The correlation set to test it — six wedges and
five faults with exact UTC timestamps, hostnames and RAS-identified lagging units — is in
[comment 5204902541](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5204902541).
Blocked on Prometheus/Grafana read access: from inside the container Xid is unreachable (`dmesg`
needs `CAP_SYSLOG`, `/dev/kmsg` is absent, `dcgmi` is not in the image, NVML never exposes Xid).

The sharpest single test: `ep-8rack`'s lagging unit was a **single GPU** (rank 173 = task 43, GPU 1,
host `sdktxs64`), so a matching Xid should name one specific GPU rather than a whole node.

---

<details>
<summary><b>Minimization ladder, toolchain axis, method, and gotchas</b> (historical detail — click to expand)</summary>

_Statuses in this block are as of 2026-08-05 and are not maintained; several items marked "queued" or "pending" have since run. Kept for the reasoning and the operational traps, which remain valid._

### The EP64 data point — "try it with expert parallelism" has already been done

Recording this in the body because it was posted on 2026-07-30 and then lost in the thread:
the plan comment of 2026-08-04 still lists `moe_hero_ep` as something "worth running
alongside", five days after an EP64 configuration had already wedged.

[Comment 5125585656](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7344#issuecomment-5125585656):
a two-rack GB200 EP64 run (128 GPUs, `cw-us-east-08a`, launched through
`experiments.grug.moe.launch_cw_scale`) went silent after step 90 and stayed `Running` until
killed 879 s later. Across 33,830 log lines: no `TimeoutError`, no `ncclCommAbort`, no
`NCCL WARN`, no NCCL output at all. All 32 tasks `Running`, zero failures, zero preemptions.
All eight sampled GPUs at 100% utilization drawing 198-228 W against a 1200 W limit.

**The stack is the same one the FSDP wedge shows.** faulthandler dumps on two different tasks
both put the main thread in `jax/_src/array.py:614 _value` <- `array.py:304 __int__` <-
`train.py:584`, materialising `int(state.step)` while the next asynchronously dispatched step
had not completed.

Non-determinism matches too: this attempt wedged at step 90, earlier ones at 38 and 145, and
one 100-step run completed clean.

**What it establishes.** The wedge does not require FSDP, does not require the vendored
attention/MoE kernels of the hero config, and does not require more than two racks. The
collective structure can change completely — expert-axis all-to-all instead of replica-axis
all-gather — and the symptom is unchanged.

**What it does not establish.** EP64 is a *different program*, not a subtraction from the FSDP
ladder, so it cannot be read as a rung verdict. It is a second, independent reproduction.

**Two knobs it rules out as necessary**, both of which differ between the two wedging programs:

| knob | FSDP hero (wedges) | EP64 2-rack (wedges) |
|---|---|---|
| `JAX_ENABLE_PGLE` | `1` | unset -> JAX default `False` |
| `--xla_gpu_experimental_parallel_collective_overlap_limit` | unset -> XLA default `1` | `4` |

Since both wedge, neither PGLE nor the collective-overlap limit is necessary in either
direction. (Note the XLA default is **1**, so the FSDP hero already runs collectives at the
*most* serialized setting.)

**What both share, and what therefore survives:** `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_ALLOCATOR=cuda_async`
(set explicitly in the EP64 repro command and forced in the FSDP trainer), command buffers
disabled per #5675, and the whole toolchain — NCCL 2.28.9, jax/jaxlib 0.11.0, driver
595.71.05, `cw-us-east-08a`. The allocator has never been ablated in either program.

**Practical consequence:** there is a ~20-minute two-rack reproduction available, against the
~87-minute twelve-rack vehicle currently in use. Multi-rack placement needs #7753 or the two
racks are split 14+18 across NVLink domains instead of 16+16.

### Ladder (cumulative — each rung keeps all previously accepted cuts)

| Rung | Cut | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `num_layers` 48 → **1** | ✅ **wedged** — step 29 @ 7.24 min; step 75 @ 9.27 min |
| 1 | `attention_implementation="reference"`, `moe_implementation="scatter"`, `expert_chunks=1` | ✅ **wedged** — step 78 @ 7.42 min |
| 2 | **synthetic tokens** (drops GCS, tokenized cache, block shuffle, mixture) | ✅ **wedged** — step 2458 @ 86.7 min |
| **2.5** | **`offload_opt_state=False`** | ⚠️ **unresolved** — runs fine (the old "cannot run" verdict is retracted), but was pre-empted by a #7956 fault at step 300 before it could wedge |
| **3** | **`JAX_ENABLE_PGLE=0`** | ⚠️ **unresolved** — censored by #7956 faults at steps 7 and 110 |
| 4 | `sconv=False`, `rope_fused=False` | pending |
| 5 | optimizer MuonH → plain Adam | pending |
| 6 | disable `watch` callback / wandb tracker | pending |
| 7 | FSDP off (replicate) | pending |
| 8 | standalone JAX + NCCL, no marin | goal |

**Rungs are currently being right-censored by #7956** (single-rank `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_INSTRUCTION`). That is a *competing risk*, not a rung verdict: a run that dies of #7956 before wedging tells you nothing about whether that rung wedges. Two rungs in a row were lost this way. Null stop rule adopted: one **uninterrupted** attempt reaching both 4.5 h and >=7500 steps with `failures` unchanged and 192/192 alive; any #7956 crash resets both clocks (exposure must not be aggregated across attempts).

**Rung 2 moved the denominator a lot: 86.7 min vs 7.42 min, ~12x.** Every rung after this needs exposure budgeted against ~87 min, not ~8. Running rung 2.5 for 25 minutes and calling a null would be meaningless.

Rack reduction (12 → 8 → 4 → 2) was deliberately **deprioritized** — hazard appears to scale with rack count, so it shrinks the repro's cost but not the hypothesis space. **Worth revisiting:** the EP64 result above wedged at two racks in ~20 min, so a cheap repro demonstrably exists on at least one program.

### Second axis: toolchain

The ladder shrinks *what code runs*; this varies *what runs it*, holding code fixed. It is not a rung — it composes with whatever the most-minimized wedging config is.

| Step | Change | Status |
|---|---|---|
| T1 | `nvidia-nccl-cu13` 2.28.9 → **2.30.7** | queued |
| T2 | run on an NVIDIA NGC JAX image (`nvcr.io/nvidia/jax:26.07-py3`) | wired, ready to launch |

Both outcomes here are informative, unlike the code rungs where a null is ambiguous: "still wedges on a different stack" strengthens every downstream claim, "does not wedge" redirects the investigation.

Three traps, all of which would have produced a **silent no-op**:

- **`uv sync --frozen`** (`iris/cluster/setup_scripts.py:77`) means a `pyproject.toml` change alone is ignored — the lock must be regenerated too.
- **GPU tasks resolve the `gpu` extra → `jax[cuda13]`, so they load `nvidia-nccl-cu13`.** `nvidia-nccl-cu12` is also in the lock and is *inert* for JAX. Overriding cu12 would have been a no-op measured as a result.
- **The task runs in a uv-created venv, not the image's Python**, so `jax`/`jaxlib`/NCCL/cuDNN arrive as pip wheels *regardless of the container image*. Swapping the image alone changes the base OS and driver userspace while leaving the entire JAX/XLA/NCCL stack byte-identical. T2 required changing dependency resolution, not just the image: `$IRIS_VENV` is now built as a `--system-site-packages` overlay on the image interpreter, with the locked closure installed minus everything the image owns (269 → 221 requirements).

Verification is by `/proc/self/maps`, not package metadata — the only trustworthy answer to "which libnccl is this process actually using". Baseline captured on a default run: `nvidia-nccl-cu13=2.28.9`, `mapped=.../nvidia/nccl/lib/libnccl.so.2`, `resolved_from_venv=['jax','jaxlib']`. A successful T2 must show jax resolving from *outside* the venv.

T1 is **not fully surgical**: `torch` also depends on `nvidia-nccl-cu12`, so the override moves torch too (+265/-39 in `uv.lock`). torch performs no collectives here, so it is a distant confound rather than a live alternative — but a positive result should be reported as "NCCL is the leading explanation", with torch pinned back before any causal claim.

### Method

This is test-case minimization, not causal attribution. **Still wedges** → accept the cut and continue. **Does not wedge** → revert and try the next; that is *not* proof of cause, since a null is weaker evidence than a reproduction.

Two rules that matter more than the ordering:

1. **Stop on wall-clock, not steps.** Step time has moved 18.6 s → 1.26 s across rungs, so a step budget silently gives a fast rung almost no exposure.
2. **Re-measure the rate after every accepted cut.** A cut that halves the hazard makes the *next* rung produce a false "fixed it" against a stale denominator. Rung 2's 12x shift is exactly this hazard, and it is now the binding constraint on the whole campaign.

### Gotchas that cost real time

- **Grep for `cuMemAllocAsync failed`, not just `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`/`out of memory`.** The allocator-level failure above uses different wording and is non-fatal, so it appears in neither the crash path nor the obvious greps.
- `iris job logs --since-seconds N --max-lines M` returns the **earliest** M lines unless you pass `--tail`. Without it a truncated fetch looks exactly like log silence. A fetch that returns exactly `--max-lines` lines hit the cap and proves nothing about absence. `--since-ms` was also observed returning a recent window rather than the requested one.
- `num_layers=0` does not build: `ArrayStacked.init` calls `jnp.stack` on an empty key list. The forward pass would tolerate it (`lax.scan` over length 0 is a no-op); only the construction site needs fixing.
- `expert_chunks != 1` requires `moe_implementation="sonic_cute"`, so dropping the vendored MoE kernel forces `expert_chunks=1` with it.
- Config dry-runs lower a broken model happily — validation never constructs it. Runtime failures need a real launch, or a local construction test.
- **Synthetic examples must be built on the host CPU device.** levanter's `CausalLmDataset` wraps construction in `eqx.filter_jit` with `with_sharding_constraint(..., SingleDeviceSharding(cpu))` (`levanter/data/text/datasets.py:150-163`); building them eagerly instead puts every prefetched example in HBM and OOMs. This is legal *only* off the mesh context — the DataLoader traces on a daemon thread whose contextvars are empty (`levanter/utils/thread_utils.py:39-46`). Calling the same function from the main thread under `set_mesh` raises `Received incompatible devices for jitted computation`.


</details>

<details>
<summary><b>Original report, 2026-07-17 by @ClassicLarry</b> (click to expand)</summary>

The 512-GPU (8-rack GB200) grug MoE datakit run silently froze at step 145 of 500. All 128 ranks reported `145it/500it` progress at exactly `20260717 20:49:47 UTC` and then went completely silent — no rank has logged anything since (confirmed ~20 min later, job still in `running` state). This is a hard hang, not a slowdown.

The hang emits **no error of any kind**: no traceback, no OOM/`RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`, no `kAllToAll` rendezvous error, and no NCCL / watchdog / CUDA / timeout message anywhere in the logs. Throughput was healthy right up to the freeze (last logged step 145 at **22.96% MFU, 2.85M tok/s**, loss 2.53).

### Why it looks like a transient collective hang, not a code bug

- **All 128 ranks froze at the same instant.** Every task's last log line is `20:49:47`. A crashed rank would let the others keep spinning and eventually NCCL-timeout; instead all ranks stopped together, which is the signature of every rank blocked inside one collective that never completes.
- **Not the data loader.** The `Data loading is taking a long time` warnings all clustered at ~20:19 (≈step 100) and stopped at `20:19:27` — none in the 30 minutes before the freeze. That warning reprints every 10s while a loader is blocked, so its absence means data was flowing at step 145.
- **The stall step is non-deterministic across runs.** An earlier datakit run wedged at step 38; a slim-pajama run completed all 100 steps clean; this one wedged at 145. A deterministic sharding/XLA bug would wedge at the *same* step every time. Non-deterministic → most likely a transient network/NVLink/IB event on one of the 8 GB200 racks that hung a collective and dragged the whole 512-GPU mesh with it.

This is a distinct failure from the compile-time `kAllToAll` wedge that was root-caused to the embedding gather and already fixed on this branch (`rematWarn=0`, `a2a=0` throughout).

### Operational gap

A hung collective is not a process failure, so Iris's `max_retries_failure=3` never triggers — the job sits idle on 512 GPUs indefinitely until killed manually. We should wire an NCCL collective timeout / watchdog so a stuck collective **aborts** the process (→ becomes a retryable failure) instead of hanging silently, turning this class of event into auto-recovery.

### Environment

- **Branch:** https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/grug/embedding-gather-shard-map (HEAD `a33e16ce`)
- **Cluster:** `marin` (CoreWeave cw-us-east-02a), 128 × GB200 nodes (4 GPU/node) = 512 GPU, 8 racks
- **Iris job:** https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Flarry%2Fgb200-d5120-512gpu-r8-datakit-500-v5-coord
- **wandb:** https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/gb200-d5120-512gpu-r8-datakit-500-v5

### Model / run

d5120, 48 layers, 64 experts pick-4, heads 40 / kv 10, head_dim 128, intermediate 2560, shared-expert 5120, vocab 128256, seq 4096 with 2048 sliding window, long-rope off. MuonH optimizer (peak lr 0.0421, linear decay to 5%, 1% warmup). Mesh `replica_axis_size=8`, `expert_axis_size=1`. FA4 (`gpu_fa4_cute`) + sonic_cute MoE, scanned layers. Batch 8192 seq × 4096 = 33.5M tokens/step (16.8B tokens over 500 steps).

### Launch command

```bash
RUN_ID=gb200-d5120-512gpu-r8-datakit-500-v5 \
SCALE_GPU_TYPE=GB200 SCALE_GPUS_PER_NODE=4 SCALE_GPU_REPLICAS=128 \
SCALE_REPLICA_AXIS=8 SCALE_EXPERT_AXIS=1 SCALE_PROCESSES_PER_TASK=1 \
SCALE_HIDDEN_DIM=5120 SCALE_NUM_LAYERS=48 SCALE_NUM_EXPERTS=64 SCALE_TOP_K=4 \
SCALE_SEQ_LEN=4096 SCALE_BATCH=8192 SCALE_STEPS=500 \
SCALE_SCAN_LAYERS=1 SCALE_MOE_IMPL=sonic_cute SCALE_ATTN_IMPL=gpu_fa4_cute \
SCALE_OPTIMIZER=muonh SCALE_DATA=datakit SCALE_TRACKER=wandb \
uv run python experiments/grug/moe/launch_cw_scale.py
```



</details>

issue.title: grug 512-GPU (8-rack GB200) run silently hangs mid-training (collective wedge, no error)

issue.body:
### Description

On a host where only some GPUs are joined by NVLink, the processes of one multi-process job (one process per GPU) compute different persistent compilation cache keys for the same program that spans them. Process 0 is the only one that writes the cache. So on the next run, the processes whose GPU has process 0's NVLink link count load the executable, and the others miss and compile. A rank that compiles while its peers loaded then waits forever in XLA's sharded autotuning for shares nobody sends, and the peers wait in the program's collectives. The whole job hangs.

**1. The key embeds the process's own GPU's NVLink link count.** `_hash_accelerator_config` (`jax/_src/cache_key.py`) hashes `xla_client.get_topology_for_devices(devices).fingerprint()`, and for a GPU that is `StreamExecutorGpuTopologyDescription::Fingerprint()`. The fingerprinted proto includes the local device's `gpu_target_config.gpu_device_info`, whose `device_interconnect_info` (field 29) carries `active_links`, the NVLink link count read through NVML. openxla/xla#40177 made the target config device-agnostic by removing the PCI bus ID and NVLink UUIDs, but `active_links` stays.

On 4x RTX 3090 (GPU0-GPU1 NV4, GPU2-GPU3 PHB), decoding each process's topology proto shows one difference: `active_links = 4` on GPU0 and GPU1, absent on GPU2 and GPU3. The processes on GPU0 and GPU1 fingerprint alike, as do those on GPU2 and GPU3, and the two pairs differ. For one 4-process SPMD program, the computation, compile options, flags and backend hash the same on every rank, and only the accelerator-config component differs between the pairs. The GPU cache key already strips the device assignment "to use cache key as invariant between processes" (`cache_key.get`), and this component breaks that invariant.

**2. A rank that compiles while its peers loaded waits forever in sharded autotuning.** With `--xla_gpu_shard_autotuning` (on by default), a compile of a program that spans processes splits its autotuning over them, and each process blocks in the coordination service's key-value store until the others' shares arrive. A rank that compiles alone waits for shares that never come. A one-device program never waits this way, because its compile takes `process_count` from its own devices.

The same hang happens in a real job. Stacks dumped at 150 s from a four-process training job with the cache on show every rank in `backend_compile_and_load`, in two different programs that both span the pool. Ranks 0 and 1 loaded the initial-state program from the cache and are compiling the train step. Ranks 2 and 3 missed the initial-state program and are compiling it. Each pair waits for autotuning shares of a program the other pair isn't compiling, and all four GPUs sit idle. A three-process trainer on GPUs 0-2 hung the same way in its first compile.

**Reproduction.** Plain `jax.distributed.initialize`, one process per GPU, with GPU1 (NVLink) and GPU2 (no NVLink) sharing one new cache directory. Each process compiles `local`, a matmul chain on its own GPU, then `pool`, the same chain over a batch split across both processes, and prints its topology fingerprint and each compile's key and hit or miss. `run.sh 1,2` runs it cold, then warm over the same directory, each run bounded to 150 s here.

<details><summary>repro.py</summary>

```python
import logging
import os
import sys
import time

rank = int(sys.argv[1])
gpus = sys.argv[2].split(",")
os.environ["CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES"] = gpus[rank]
os.environ["JAX_ENABLE_COMPILATION_CACHE"] = "true"
os.environ["JAX_COMPILATION_CACHE_DIR"] = os.environ["REPRO_CACHE"]
os.environ["JAX_PERSISTENT_CACHE_MIN_COMPILE_TIME_SECS"] = "0"
os.environ["JAX_PERSISTENT_CACHE_MIN_ENTRY_SIZE_BYTES"] = "-1"

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np
from jax._src.lib import xla_client
from jax.sharding import NamedSharding, PartitionSpec as P


class Keys(logging.Handler):
    """Prints each compile's cache key and whether the persistent cache held it."""

    def emit(self, record):
        message = record.getMessage()
        if "cache hit for" in message or "CACHE MISS for" in message:
            module = message.split("'")[1]
            key = message.rsplit("'", 2)[-2]
            print(f"[{rank}] {'hit ' if 'hit for' in message else 'miss'} {module} key ...{key[-12:]}", flush=True)


logger = logging.getLogger("jax._src.compiler")
logger.setLevel(logging.DEBUG)
logger.addHandler(Keys())
logger.propagate = False

jax.distributed.initialize(coordinator_address=f"127.0.0.1:{os.environ['REPRO_PORT']}",
                           num_processes=len(gpus), process_id=rank)
fingerprint = xla_client.get_topology_for_devices(jax.local_devices()).fingerprint()
print(f"[{rank}] GPU{gpus[rank]} topology fingerprint {fingerprint:016x}, jax {jax.__version__}", flush=True)


def local(x, w):
    for _ in range(6):
        x = jnp.tanh(x @ w)
    return jnp.sum(x)


def pool(x, w):
    for _ in range(6):
        x = jnp.tanh(x @ w)
    return jnp.sum(x)


began = time.perf_counter()
device = jax.local_devices()[0]
value = float(jax.jit(local)(jax.device_put(np.ones((2048, 1536), np.float32), device),
                             jax.device_put(np.eye(1536, dtype=np.float32) * 0.5, device)))
print(f"[{rank}] local ran in {time.perf_counter() - began:.1f}s: {value}", flush=True)

mesh = jax.make_mesh((jax.device_count(),), ("data",))
x = jax.make_array_from_process_local_data(NamedSharding(mesh, P("data")),
                                           np.ones((2048, 1536), np.float32) * (1 + rank))
w = jax.device_put(np.eye(1536, dtype=np.float32) * 0.5, NamedSharding(mesh, P()))
began = time.perf_counter()
value = float(jax.jit(pool)(x, w))
print(f"[{rank}] pool ran in {time.perf_counter() - began:.1f}s: {value}", flush=True)
```
</details>

<details><summary>run.sh</summary>

```bash
# run.sh <gpus> [python]: repro.py's cold run, then its warm run over the same new cache directory,
# one process per GPU of the comma-separated <gpus>, each run bounded to REPRO_SECONDS (240).
gpus=$1
python=${2:-python}
here=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)
cache=$(mktemp -d "${REPRO_CACHE_ROOT:-/tmp}/repro-cache.XXXX")
count=$(echo "$gpus" | tr , '\n' | wc -l)
for run in cold warm; do
    port=$((20000 + RANDOM % 20000))
    began=$(date +%s)
    echo "== $run run over $cache"
    for ((rank = 0; rank < count; rank++)); do
        REPRO_CACHE=$cache REPRO_PORT=$port timeout -k 10 "${REPRO_SECONDS:-240}" "$python" "$here/repro.py" $rank "$gpus" 2>&1 \
            | grep -E "^\[[0-9]+\] " &
    done
    wait
    echo "== $run run took $(($(date +%s) - began)) s"
done
rm -rf "$cache"
```
</details>

Output with jax 0.11.2, `REPRO_SECONDS=150 bash run.sh 1,2`. In the warm run rank 0 loads `pool` and rank 1 misses it, and neither prints `pool ran` before the bound kills them:

```
== cold run over /workspace/scratch/dist-inference/repro-cache.gmSA
[1] GPU2 topology fingerprint d5bfe87ebbdab996, jax 0.11.2
[1] miss jit_local key ...f2ce2b8e3236
[1] local ran in 2.6s: 44397.05859375
[1] miss jit__identity_fn key ...cda6d34a8077
[1] miss jit_pool key ...c15ec8a6e12a
[1] pool ran in 0.6s: 114849.296875
[0] GPU1 topology fingerprint 2834ad2e578f5a6a, jax 0.11.2
[0] miss jit_local key ...e63b23ca61de
[0] local ran in 2.8s: 44397.05859375
[0] miss jit__identity_fn key ...dac62f07b528
[0] miss jit_pool key ...51c54fe47207
[0] pool ran in 0.6s: 114849.296875
== cold run took 7 s
== warm run over /workspace/scratch/dist-inference/repro-cache.gmSA
[1] GPU2 topology fingerprint d5bfe87ebbdab996, jax 0.11.2
[1] miss jit_local key ...f2ce2b8e3236
[1] local ran in 0.6s: 44397.05859375
[1] miss jit__identity_fn key ...cda6d34a8077
[1] miss jit_pool key ...c15ec8a6e12a
[0] GPU1 topology fingerprint 2834ad2e578f5a6a, jax 0.11.2
[0] hit  jit_local key ...e63b23ca61de
[0] local ran in 0.1s: 44397.05859375
[0] hit  jit__identity_fn key ...dac62f07b528
[0] hit  jit_pool key ...51c54fe47207
== warm run took 160 s
```

The same program on GPUs 0,1 or 2,3, whose processes fingerprint alike, runs warm on both processes. A smaller program doesn't always hang: in one jitted step of four 1024x1024 bf16 matmuls on GPUs 1,2, the rank that missed compiled alone and finished. Its keys differed the same way.

**Expected.** One cache decision per computation: every process of it loads, or every process compiles, so `jax_share_binary_between_hosts` also keeps working on hosts like this. Separately, sharded autotuning could fail after a bounded wait with an error that names the missing shares, rather than hang.

**Proposed fix**, carried on AshishKumar4/jax branch `cache-key-pool-fingerprints` (0afcd84c, on main), with a 0.11.2 carry on `v0.11.2-cache-key-pool-fingerprints` (19a48d1d):

- Each process publishes, once through the distributed runtime client, its topology fingerprint and its accelerators: platform and runtime version, the CUDA driver, cuDNN and cuBLAS versions, and each local device's kind, compute capability and core count. It reads each peer's once.
- For a computation that spans processes, if every process names the same accelerators, `_hash_accelerator_config` hashes the sorted set of their fingerprints, so every process computes one key. Links don't change an executable that spans processes: at this XLA revision `active_links` reaches compilation only through the SOL latency estimator (Hopper, Blackwell and MI300), the analytical estimator (off by default) and the collective kernels (every replica local to one process).
- If the processes name different accelerators, the computation gets no key. `_get_cache_key` already turns that into compiling without the cache on every process, and it logs which processes have which accelerators. Sharing would load code built for another GPU.

With it, the same `run.sh 1,2` gives one key on both ranks, and the warm run loads it on both:

```
== warm run over /workspace/scratch/dist-inference/repro-cache.ztBX
[0] GPU1 topology fingerprint 2834ad2e578f5a6a, jax 0.11.2.post3
[0] hit  jit_local key ...e63b23ca61de
[0] local ran in 0.1s: 44397.05859375
[0] hit  jit__identity_fn key ...eaec7e237ec8
[0] hit  jit_pool key ...b63357934d79
[0] pool ran in 0.0s: 114849.296875
[1] GPU2 topology fingerprint d5bfe87ebbdab996, jax 0.11.2.post3
[1] miss jit_local key ...f2ce2b8e3236
[1] local ran in 0.6s: 44397.05859375
[1] hit  jit__identity_fn key ...eaec7e237ec8
[1] hit  jit_pool key ...b63357934d79
[1] pool ran in 0.0s: 114849.296875
== warm run took 3 s
```

`jit_local` runs on one process, so it keeps its per-process key, and only process 0 writes it. Rank 1 recompiling it is harmless: a one-device compile doesn't shard its autotuning.

The four-process training job gives the same picture with the fix. Every program that spans the pool loads on every process, and the warm start reaches its first step in 14.2 s against 69.3 s cold. Two processes of two GPUs each take 13.0 s against 63.0 s, and GPUs 1,2 take 13.5 s against 63.5 s. Processes whose fingerprint differs from process 0's still compile their few one-process programs, as rank 1 does `jit_local` above.

Coverage:

| Case | Key with the fix | How it was checked |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Processes that differ only in links (this issue) | one key per computation | this repro on GPUs 1,2 and 0,3, and on 4 processes over GPUs 0-3: warm loads everywhere; unit tests with fake fingerprints |
| Processes on different accelerators (architecture, runtime, driver, cuDNN, cuBLAS, kind, cores) | no key; compiled without the cache on every process, logged | unit tests with fake records; not on hardware |
| Processes whose fingerprints differ only in fields not in the accelerators string (clocks, memory, ECC, CUB, toolkit) | shared | not covered: a residual, bounded by `GpuDeviceInfoProto`'s fields |
| Processes that fingerprint alike (a homogeneous GPU cluster) | unchanged: a one-element set hashes the same 8 bytes | GPUs 0,1 and 2,3 give the same key as jax 0.11.2; unit test |
| A single process, or no distributed client (e.g. single controller) | unchanged: the old path | same hash as jax 0.11.2 on an RTX 3090 (1 and 4 devices), on CPU, and on a TPU v6e (1 chip) |
| TPU multi-host slice | unchanged if every host's fingerprint is the same | unverified: the TPU client's topology code isn't public |
| Cost | one publish per process and one read per peer, per distributed client | unit test |

Workarounds: `JAX_ENABLE_COMPILATION_CACHE=false` for multi-process GPU jobs. `--xla_gpu_shard_autotuning=false` ends the wait, but then ranks can run different executables (loaded on some, freshly autotuned on others), which is openxla/xla#7716's deadlock.

Related: openxla/xla#49371 (the XLA side: the GPU topology fingerprint hashes one local device's links), #33852 (a rare hang with one process stuck compiling while the others wait at the next sync; this mechanism would produce that picture), marin-community/marin#9042 (the same wait in XLA's autotuner when ranks lower different HLO), openxla/xla#7716, openxla/xla#40177.
